name: Environmental Defense Fund: climate (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: a tonne of greenhouse gas kept out of the air spares people everywhere, so the result is spread by world population; the small US power-plant and vehicle smoke share is left in the world figure.
summary: The Environmental Defense Fund (EDF; New York, with offices in Europe, China, India, Mexico, Indonesia and Japan) uses science, economics, law and advocacy for environmental policy; this model covers its climate and regional work ($120.6M in its year to September 2025, $169M with its share of core capacities) and counts the largest climate policies it worked on that were won in October 2021 to September 2025 (EPA's oil and gas methane rule, the EU Methane Regulation, EPA's power-plant and vehicle standards) and its MethaneSAT satellite, lost after 15 months, whose cost is added to the period's. At the defaults a dollar given averts about 0.0035 tonnes of CO₂e (about $290 a tonne), 0.0018 years of healthy life per $1,000, nearly all of it from the two methane rules, whose tonnes count for methane's own, earlier warming and the ozone it forms; it is low because each win is shared with many groups and with what governments would have done anyway (EDF is credited with 8% to 25% of the advocacy behind each), the US rules have since been delayed or repealed, and EDF's climate spending is large. The biggest uncertainties are the shared years a won reform counts, the missing-data discount and how much of each win was advocacy's doing; every branch is discounted for missing data, since no tonne is measured for its work.

rows.label: EPA vehicle standards: tonnes of CO₂ a year
MethaneSAT: oil and gas methane worldwide, tonnes of CO₂e a year
rows.explainer: The pool MethaneSAT's data could act on: the world's oil and gas operations emit about 80 million tonnes of methane a year (IEA Global Methane Tracker, 2024 and 2025 editions), 2.4 billion tonnes of CO₂e at the GWP100 of 29.8 the shared facts use. Our judgment, 2.4 billion (2.0 to 2.9), the range for the inventories' spread.

rows.label: MethaneSAT: share of that methane cut because of its data
rows.explainer: MethaneSAT measured large oil and gas regions from March 2024 until contact was lost in June 2025 and published its maps (Permian and other US basins, Central Asia, the Middle East; methane intensities two to three times the inventories in several). No regulator or company has reported a cut traced to its data; its value was to be enforcement and the EU's import rule's measurement, which the loss cut short (its aircraft, MethaneAIR, and the data already taken carry on). Our judgment, 0.02% of the world's oil and gas methane for the years below (0.002% to 0.2%), anchored on its 15 months of data from regions holding a large part of the emissions and on other satellites (TROPOMI, GHGSat, Carbon Mapper) doing much the same work.

rows.label: Share of each win due to advocacy at all (all groups together)
rows.explainer: The shared figure (facts: climate.advocacy_share_of_policy_win, 30%, 10% to 60%): the part of a won policy that is the advocates' doing rather than what governments, industry and events would have done. Every policy win below takes it, as in Clean Air Task Force's model; EDF's part of the advocates' work is each branch's attribution row. The wins are in, so this is not a chance of winning. MethaneSAT is EDF's own work and doesn't take it.

Evidence adjustment: how far the regulators' and modellers' tonnes should be trusted
rows.explainer: The tonnes are ex-ante estimates by the regulators (EPA) and modellers (Oeko-Institut), not measured cuts; regulators' estimates of a rule's cuts are sometimes too high (compliance short of the rule) and sometimes too low (leaks larger than inventories say, as EDF's own studies found). Our judgment, 0.8 (0.5 to 1.1), applied to every branch; delivery and repeal are in each branch's implementation row.

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this win (50%, 20% to 85%), as in Clean Air Task Force's model: trade reshuffling and the US rule's overlap taken out.

rows.label: EU Methane Regulation: EDF's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: EDF Europe (Brussels, London, Amsterdam) campaigned for the regulation and its import standard, and EDF's science underpins it: it led the UN Climate and Clean Air Coalition's measurement studies (note 1, p. 12) and helped design OGMP 2.0, the reporting framework the regulation adopts; its Europe report says the regulation was 'adopted in 2024 with key support from EDF'. Others: Clean Air Task Force (credited 20% in its model), Bellona, ECOS, the Environmental Investigation Agency and many national groups, with industry lobbying on both sides. EDF's whole climate spending (Stabilize the Climate $99.5M and regional work $21.1M in FY2025, before core capacities and the satellite) is about three times Clean Air Task Force's whole budget ($43M in 2025). But in Brussels its team was one of a handful, and its science counts here only as advocacy. Our judgment, 15% (5% to 30%); with Clean Air Task Force's 20% that leaves 65% of the advocates' share to the others.

rows.label: EPA methane rule: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this win (80%, 60% to 100%).

rows.label: EPA methane rule: EDF's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: EDF led the field: its 16-study series with over 140 researchers (2012-2018) measured the industry's leaks at about 60% above EPA's inventory, its petitions, comments and lawsuits pushed for the rule, and it defended it in court (with others, it is suing over the 2025 delays). Others: Clean Air Task Force (credited 10% in its model), NRDC, Earthjustice, Sierra Club, Earthworks, state groups and the Moms Clean Air Force (an EDF partner whose spending sits partly in these accounts); industry lobbied against parts of the rule. EDF's whole climate spending (Stabilize the Climate $99.5M and regional work $21.1M in FY2025, before core capacities and the satellite) is about three times Clean Air Task Force's whole budget ($43M in 2025). Our judgment, 25% (12% to 40%), the largest single share; with Clean Air Task Force's 10% that leaves 65% to the others.

source.title: EDF (2025), Groups file lawsuit challenging Trump EPA final rule that delays methane pollution protections from oil and gas industry
source.note: EDF's methane studies: Alvarez et al. (2018), Assessment of methane emissions from the U.S. oil and gas supply chain, Science 361, 186-188 (emissions about 60% above EPA's inventory).

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: EDF's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: EDF was a party in West Virginia v. EPA (2022) and argued for strong standards after it; NRDC, Sierra Club (Beyond Coal, the field's largest campaign), Earthjustice, Clean Air Task Force (credited 10% in its model) and others did too, and the utilities' and coal states' lobbying was larger. Our judgment, 10% (4% to 25%).

rows.label: EPA power-plant standards: share of credit used
EPA power-plant standards: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: The shared figure for this win (5%, 1% to 20%): repealed in September 2026.

rows.label: EPA vehicle standards: share of the tonnes that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Share of EPA's estimate that wouldn't have happened anyway: carmakers' own electric-vehicle plans, California's and other states' rules and the tax credits then in force would have cut part of the tonnes; EPA's baseline holds the earlier standards. Our judgment, 70% (40% to 90%).

rows.label: EPA vehicle standards: EDF's share of the advocacy resources behind the win
rows.explainer: EDF's legal and transport teams pressed for the standards and defended earlier ones in court, beside NRDC, Sierra Club, the Union of Concerned Scientists, the American Lung Association, the ICCT's analysis and many others; carmakers and dealers lobbied on both sides. Our judgment, 8% (3% to 20%).

rows.label: EPA vehicle standards: share of credit used
EPA vehicle standards: share of the win's tonnes delivered
rows.explainer: EPA rescinded the endangerment finding and repealed every vehicle greenhouse-gas standard in February 2026 (effective April 2026); the 2025 budget law also ended the electric-vehicle credits. What remains is the chance the courts restore the standards or a later administration reissues them within the years counted. Our judgment, 5% (1% to 20%), like the repealed power-plant standards.

source.title: Jones Day (2026), EPA finalizes repeal of greenhouse gas endangerment finding
source.note: Signed 12 February 2026, published 18 February 2026 (91 Fed. Reg. 7686), effective 20 April 2026; repeals all motor-vehicle greenhouse-gas standards.

rows.label: MethaneSAT: share of the cut that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: Other satellites and aircraft (TROPOMI, GHGSat, Carbon Mapper, the UN's methane alert system) find many of the same large sources. Our judgment, 70% (40% to 90%).

rows.label: MethaneSAT: EDF's share of the resources behind the data
rows.explainer: MethaneSAT was EDF's project, paid for mostly by donors in these accounts; partners added resources: New Zealand's government and space agency, Harvard and the Smithsonian (science), Google (data processing), and the companies and regulators who must act on the data. Our judgment, 60% (40% to 80%).

rows.label: MethaneSAT: share of credit used
MethaneSAT: share of the data's planned use delivered
rows.explainer: The satellite worked for about 15 of its planned 60 or more months, so the routine monitoring the cut share assumes for its years was cut short; the data already taken and processed is still released. Our judgment, 60% (30% to 90%).

rows.label: Counted less where the outcome isn't measured for this charity
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): no tonne is measured for EDF's work; the tonnes are regulators' and modellers' estimates of whole policies and its part in them a judgment, and MethaneSAT's cut is a judgment. Every branch takes it.

rows.label: Other wins of the period not modelled, as a share of the modelled value
rows.explainer: The five branches are EDF's largest climate wins of the period with published tonnes, but much of the spending went elsewhere: the Inflation Reduction Act (2022; EDF and EDF Action, its 501(c)(4) inside these accounts, campaigned for it among hundreds of groups; most of its clean-power credits were cut back in 2025); the IRA's methane fee (repealed in 2025, worth nothing now); EPA's heavy-duty truck standards (repealed with the vehicle rules); state laws (clean power and rate cases in 2025); the regional teams' work in China (its carbon market), India (agriculture and methane) and Europe (shipping, aviation, the carbon market's extension); international shipping and aviation; agricultural methane. Their spending is in the cost, so leaving them out would count them as worth nothing. Our judgment, 40% of the modelled value (15% to 100%): the modelled wins are the biggest, but the unmodelled work takes over half of the climate spending.

rows.label: Side effect: smog and toxic air pollution cut by the US methane rule, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: EPA's methane rule also cuts smog-forming volatile organic compounds near wells: EPA's analysis gives about 56 (2028) to 74 (2038) ozone deaths a year avoided from them (Tables 3-8 and 3-9), about an eighth of the rule's own heat-death value at the shared rates. The US methane rule is a larger part of this model's value than of Clean Air Task Force's (where the same step is about 1%): our estimate 1.5% (0.5% to 3%).

source.title: US EPA (2023), Regulatory Impact Analysis for the final oil and natural gas standards

rows.formula: (eumr_expected_tonnes + usmeth_expected_tonnes + msat_expected_tonnes) / (eumr_expected_tonnes + usmeth_expected_tonnes + pwr_expected_tonnes + veh_expected_tonnes + msat_expected_tonnes)
rows.explainer: The two methane rules' and MethaneSAT's share of the expected tonnes, weighted before waits and years counted (which can't feed a conversion row). The shared climate conversion values this share by methane's own, earlier warming and adds the ozone it forms (docs/normalization.md 2.5).

rows.label: Share of these tonnes from burning less fossil fuel near people
rows.explainer: Power plants and vehicles burn less fuel; methane leaks carry no fuel smoke.

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne cut from US cars and light trucks, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: US road vehicles' fine particles and ozone killed about 53,000 people in 2005 (Caiazzo et al. 2013, Atmospheric Environment 79), from about 1.5 billion tonnes of CO₂ a year, and far fewer today with cleaner engines (EPA's Tier 3 standards); per tonne that is roughly 0.05 to 0.25 of the world fossil-fuel average (1.46 per 10,000 tonnes) then, lower now, and the electricity that replaces the petrol carries some smoke of its own. Our judgment, 0.05 (0.02 to 0.15).

rows.label: Air-pollution deaths per tonne of these fuel tonnes, relative to the fossil-fuel average
rows.explainer: Per fuel and place: the power-plant standards' tonnes are coal plants' (facts: climate.us_coal_power_smoke_factor, as in Clean Air Task Force's model); the vehicle standards' are cars' (row above). Weighted by each branch's expected tonnes.

rows.label: Air pollution these tonnes cut, relative to an average fossil-fuel tonne
Air-pollution deaths averted per tonne, counted directly (none here)
rows.explainer: None counted directly: methane's ozone and earlier warming are in the shared conversion, through the methane share.

rows.formula: (eumr_downstream * eumr_total_adj + usmeth_downstream * usmeth_total_adj + pwr_downstream * pwr_total_adj + veh_downstream * veh_total_adj + msat_downstream * msat_total_adj) / period_years * (1 + unmodelled_benefits_adj + voc_health_share)
rows.explainer: Each win's expected tonnes × its own adjustments, summed, spread over the period's four years, with the other wins and the side effect added as shares.
